title: Rabbit Emoji 🐇 Meaning: Easter Bunny and Rabbit Holes
description: 🐇 means bunnies, Easter, speed and "down the rabbit hole." See where the Easter bunny came from, what the rabbit emoji means in slang, and how it differs from 🐰.
summary: The 🐇 rabbit emoji shows a whole rabbit, usually mid-hop. People use it for pet bunnies, Easter and the Easter bunny, spring, speed, and the phrase "down the rabbit hole" for getting absorbed in a topic. It also appears in "rabbit, rabbit" good-luck posts on the first of the month.
meaning: The most popular use online is the rabbit hole. Saying you "went down a 🐇🕳️" means you started reading about one thing and lost hours following links, a phrase borrowed from Alice's fall in "Alice's Adventures in Wonderland." The same book gives "follow the white rabbit," which The Matrix later made into shorthand for discovering a hidden truth.

In spring the emoji turns to Easter. The Easter bunny is a folk figure, not a biblical one: it arrived in America with German immigrants, whose Osterhase brought colored eggs to children who had been good. Hares and rabbits were long associated with spring and fertility, which made them a natural fit for the season. Many Christian families enjoy the bunny alongside church while keeping the focus of the day on the Resurrection.

Pet owners use 🐇 for their own rabbits, adoption posts and bunny care tips. Speed is another meaning, from the tortoise-and-hare fable to runners who call the pacesetter the "rabbit." "Breeding like rabbits" jokes about big families or fast multiplication. Magicians pulling a rabbit from a hat give it another meaning: a surprise solution produced at the last minute.

Two other uses are worth knowing. Some people post "rabbit, rabbit 🐇" on the first of the month for luck, an old British and New England superstition. The rabbit also has a sexual connotation through the Playboy bunny logo, though that reading needs explicit context. In ordinary messages, neither of those is the default reading.

contexts.label: At Easter
contexts.body: Egg hunts, chocolate bunnies and Easter baskets bring 🐇 out with 🥚, 🐣 and 🌷. Churches and Catholic schools often use it for children's activities after Mass, while reserving ✝️ for the religious message. Families post it with photos of kids in bunny ears.

contexts.label: Online and in texting
contexts.body: "I fell down a rabbit hole 🐇" explains a late night of research, Wikipedia browsing or conspiracy videos. It is self-deprecating rather than worrying. "Follow the white rabbit" posts hint at mysteries, ARGs or a new discovery. The phrase is affectionate about one's own habits.

contexts.label: For pet owners
contexts.body: Rabbit owners and rescues use 🐇 for adoption listings, care tips and photos of their bunnies. The full-body rabbit suits these posts better than the cartoon face, and owners often pair it with 🥕 or 🌿 for treats and greens.

contexts.label: Around the world
contexts.body: In the Chinese zodiac the Rabbit is one of the twelve animals, and Lunar New Year greetings in a Year of the Rabbit use 🐇. East Asian folklore also sees a rabbit in the moon, pounding rice or medicine, so 🐇 pairs with 🌕 at the Mid-Autumn Festival.

confusedWith.difference: 🐰 is a cartoon bunny face, cuter and more expressive, used for Easter, cuteness and affectionate messages. 🐇 is the whole animal in a more realistic pose, better for pets, speed and rabbit holes.
🐹 is a hamster face, a small rodent pet with round cheeks and short ears. People sometimes grab it for any small furry pet, but rabbits have long ears and are 🐇 or 🐰.
🐁 is a full-body mouse with a long tail. It is used for mice, pests and computer mice. Rabbits are larger, with long ears and a puff tail.

avoid: Do not use 🐇 for Christ or the meaning of Easter in a religious post; the bunny is a folk custom, and ✝️ fits better.
Be careful pairing it with suggestive emojis, where the Playboy association may be read in.
design: A whole rabbit seen from the side, usually white or light gray, with long upright or laid-back ears, a round tail and its back legs gathered as if about to hop. Designs differ in coat color and pose, with some sitting and some leaping, but every major platform shows the full animal rather than a face.

faqs.q: What is the difference between 🐇 and 🐰?
faqs.a: 🐇 is the full-body rabbit in a natural pose. 🐰 is a cute bunny face. Both work for Easter; 🐰 feels sweeter, while 🐇 suits pets, speed and "rabbit hole" jokes.

faqs.q: What does "down the rabbit hole" mean?
faqs.a: Getting deeply absorbed in a topic, usually by following one link or video after another. The phrase comes from Alice falling into Wonderland. Online it is mostly lighthearted, though it can describe drifting into conspiracy theories.

faqs.q: Is the Easter bunny in the Bible?
faqs.a: No. The Easter bunny is a folk tradition that came to America with German immigrants. Rabbits and hares were long linked to spring and new life. Christians celebrate Easter as Jesus' resurrection; the bunny is a separate custom for children.
It is a superstition: saying "rabbit, rabbit" as your first words on the first day of a month is said to bring good luck for the rest of it. Some people post it with 🐇 every month.

faqs.q: When was the rabbit emoji added?
faqs.a: 🐇 is listed under Emoji 1.0, dated 2015. The rabbit face 🐰 is listed in the earlier 0.6 set, which is why both exist.
